Doctor mode

250 adults lay in a scanner for five minutes doing nothing with their eyes open. Some live with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or ADHD. Some are control volunteers with no diagnosis. Doctors can't tell who's who from a scan like this. Think you can? Think a computer can? Make the call one patient at a time and get the answer at once. Keep score against the computer and against the laziest doctor alive. That doctor says "nothing wrong" every single time.

Day streak 4

Doctor mode

Your job: look at the averaged brain scan of three patients who share one diagnosis, and pick which of two diagnoses it is, by spotting the match.

261 real people lay in a scanner doing nothing, and 11 moved too much to use, so 250 are in the game. Some live with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or ADHD. Some have no diagnosis. Doctors cannot tell who is who from a scan like this. Can you? Can a computer? Each round gives you a stack of three patients who share one diagnosis, their scans averaged into one map, and two diagnoses on the table. Five stacks per shift.

Control volunteer means a person with no diagnosis. Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are mental health conditions that change thinking and mood. ADHD is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, trouble with focus and sitting still.

You play against the computer and against Dr. Nothing-Wrong. That doctor says "nothing wrong" whenever control volunteer is one of the two diagnoses and tosses a coin when it is not, and still is right 64 times in 100. The computer is right 71 times in 100 with two diagnoses on the table. Guessing gets 50. The map is your clue: under each diagnosis sits that group's usual map, and your job is to spot which one looks more like the stack's map. The map rule (picking the closer usual map) is right 70 times in 100, so even a good match is a nudge and not a promise. Your first stack comes with a short tour of the screen. Three free hints wait on every stack and nobody will judge you for using them.

    This part is written the way the lab writes. Skip it if you like.

    Words you will meet here
    schizophrenia
    a mental illness that can bring voices, fixed false beliefs and muddled thinking
    bipolar disorder
    a mental illness with long swings between very high and very low moods
    ADHD
    attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: trouble keeping attention and sitting still
    surgery
    an operation
    symptoms
    the signs of an illness a person notices or reports
    MRI
    a brain scanner picture, short for magnetic resonance imaging.
    psychiatric
    to do with mental health.
    median
    the middle value: half the people are above it and half are below.
    balanced
    a score where each of the four groups counts the same, however many people are in it.
    whole-region average
    one number for a whole patch of brain, the average of everything inside it.
    Default (network)
    the Default mode network, the team that is busiest when your mind wanders.
    label shuffle
    mixing up who has which diagnosis on purpose, to see what the computer scores by luck.
    mean
    the average: add the numbers up and divide by how many there are.
    rest
    lying still in the scanner with eyes open and no task.
    training
    the practice the computer gets on other people's scans and diagnoses before it guesses.
    cerebellum
    the small brain tucked under the back of the big one
    region
    one patch of brain, from a standard map of the brain cut into small pieces.
    network
    a team of regions that tend to rise and fall together.
    hubness
    how chatty a region is with all the others (the average of its link scores).
    z (Fisher z)
    a link score between two regions, stretched so it is easy to average.
    FD
    head motion, in millimeters, between one picture and the next.
    d (Cohen's d)
    how big a difference between two groups is. 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
    p
    how often luck alone would give a difference this big. Small p means luck is a poor explanation.
    raw p
    p with no correction for looking at many regions at once.
    confound
    something else that differs between the groups and can fake a brain difference, like how much people fidget.
    correlation, r
    how closely two numbers move together. r = 0 means no link, +1 means they rise together perfectly and -1 means one rises as the other falls.
    cortex, cortical
    the cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain; cortical means of the cortex.
    Default mode, Limbic
    two of the seven cortex networks: Default mode is busiest when your mind wanders, and Limbic handles emotion and memory.
    Bonferroni
    a very strict correction: a region only counts if its p is tiny, because we looked at 432 regions at once.
    false-discovery q (FDR)
    a gentler correction for looking at many regions. q is the share of "discoveries" that would be luck. A q near 1.00 means nothing stands out from luck.
    uncorrected
    a p with no correction for looking at many regions at once. About 1 region in 20 passes p under 0.05 by luck.
    SD (standard deviation)
    how spread out a set of numbers is around its average.
    standard error
    how far an average might be from the true average, because we only measured some people. The whiskers on the bars are plus and minus one.
    framewise displacement
    the same thing as FD: how far the head moved between two pictures.
    volume
    one full 3D picture of the brain. The scanner takes one every two seconds. "Brain volume" in the notes below means the 3D picture grid.
    atlas
    a standard map that cuts the brain into named pieces, so every person's brain can be split the same way.
    connection, connectome
    a connection is the link score between two regions. The connectome is all of them together.
    regress out
    use arithmetic to remove one thing (here, head motion) from another before comparing.
    percentile
    the share of a group that falls below a value. The 95th percentile is the value that 95 of 100 fall below.
    model
    the computer program that turns the clues into a guess.
    held out
    left out of the computer's training, so it is tested on a person it has never seen.
    AUC
    how well a score separates two groups. 0.50 is a coin flip, 1.00 is perfect.
    shuffle p
    how often a computer fed shuffled labels does as well as the real one.
    penalized logistic regression
    a plain, careful way to let a computer weigh thousands of clues.
    fROI read
    reading a person's own most responsive spots, the lab's stricter method.
    LH_, RH_ names
    atlas codes for regions; LH is left and RH is right.
    base rate
    the score you get by always giving the same answer (here, always saying control volunteer).
    coupling
    how much two regions rise and fall together.
    usual map
    the average hubness map of one group. When a stack is on screen, its three patients are left out of their own group's average.
    stack
    three patients who share one diagnosis, with their hubness maps averaged region by region into one map.
    match score
    the correlation (r) between two maps across the 432 regions. 0 is no match and 1 is a perfect match.
    map rule
    pick the diagnosis whose usual map matches the stack's map best, by the match score.
    practice rounds
    rounds drawn by the build script exactly the way the game draws them, to measure how often a rule is right.
    two options, two-option
    a round with two diagnoses on the table, the real one and one other at random; guessing gets 50 in 100.
    coin toss
    picking one of the two options at random.
    out-of-fold
    a score the computer gave a person while that person was held out of its training.
    paper words
    the three topics that brain-imaging papers most often link to a region, from the Neurosynth database.
    Visual, Body and movement, Attention, Salience, Control
    five of the seven cortex networks: Visual handles seeing, Body and movement handles touch and moving, Attention points your focus, Salience notices what matters right now, and Control plans and holds things in mind.
    tumors, strokes
    a tumor is a lump of cells growing where it should not, and a stroke is damage from blood not reaching part of the brain.
    inflammation
    the body's swelling and defense reaction, which can also touch the brain.
    medication
    medicine a person takes, which can change how the brain behaves in the scanner.
    cigarettes
    smoking, which can also change how the brain behaves in the scanner.
    one-vs-control
    comparing one diagnosis group against the control volunteers, one group at a time.
    fold
    one strip of the cerebellum, the small brain at the back. Region names such as fold VI or fold Crus I say which strip.
    Neurosynth
    a database that reads thousands of brain-imaging papers and notes which brain spots each topic word goes with.
    The short version

    We compared the resting brains of four groups. Some brain differences show up, but they are small and they overlap a lot. With all four diagnoses on the table the computer gets about half of the people right, and mostly by saying "control volunteer." With two on the table it is right 71 times in 100, where guessing gets 50. Nobody can diagnose a person from this kind of scan yet.

    Read this first

    The round. A stack of 3 patients who share one diagnosis, their hubness maps averaged region by region into one map, and two diagnoses: the real one and one other drawn at random. Each of the four groups has a usual map, the mean hubness map of its people, and all 3 patients of the stack are left out of their own group's average, so the answer cannot copy itself. The round screen shows the two usual maps under the two diagnoses with no scores, so the player matches by eye. Averaging three patients washes out some of each person's noise; each person has only one rest scan, so the stack is three different people.

    The map rule. A computer doing the comparison picks the diagnosis whose usual map matches the stack's map best over all 432 regions, by the match score (the correlation r between the two maps, from -1 to 1), and the feedback card shows those two scores. In 5000 practice rounds drawn the way the game draws them (20 per patient, each with two more patients of the same diagnosis and one other diagnosis) that rule is right 70 times in 100, where guessing gets 50. Over the 400 cortex regions alone it is right 69 times in 100 and over the 32 cerebellum regions alone 58, so the rule uses all 432 regions. By network it is Visual 60, Body and movement 63, Attention 57, Salience 60, Limbic 52, Control 65, Default mode 63, Cerebellum 58. Taking the all-people average out of both maps first gives 66. The rule clears the bar of 60 (guessing plus 10), so the small maps are shown as a clue. It is a nudge and not a diagnosis.

    The opponents on the same practice rounds. The computer (its out-of-fold probabilities averaged over the 3 patients, then the diagnosis with the higher of the two) is right 71 times in 100. Dr. Nothing-Wrong says control volunteer whenever it is one of the two and tosses a coin when it is not, and is right 64 times in 100, because 118 of the 250 people are control volunteers.

    How the round got here. The game started with four diagnoses per patient: the map rule was right 41 times in 100 (guessing got 25), the computer 50 and Dr. Nothing-Wrong 47, and players scored about 1 or 2 of 5. The next form had two diagnoses and one patient, with the usual maps as the clue: the map rule was right 62 times in 100, the computer 70 and Dr. Nothing-Wrong 65. Averaging 3 patients of one diagnosis lifted the map rule to 70 (the computer to 71, Dr. Nothing-Wrong 64), so the round became a stack.

    Do the groups differ at all?

    This map is patients minus controls region by region in standard-deviation units (Cohen's d). Red means more in patients and blue means less. The slider sets how picky you are about evidence. A region is painted only if its raw uncorrected p is under the bar. Loosen it and watch the map fill up. Be careful. At p < 0.05 about 5 % of the 432 regions light up by pure luck.

     

    The fidget problem

    This is the oldest trap in brain imaging: a confound, meaning something else that differs between the groups and can fake a brain difference. The bars show how far each head moved between pictures as mean framewise displacement in mm averaged per group. The whiskers are ± 1 standard error. Fidget more and your whole connectome looks "different". People who moved more than 0.5 mm on average were left out.
    groupnleft outmean FD (SD)medianvolumes > 0.5 mmvs controls
    control volunteer11840.141 (0.084)0.1123 %–
    schizophrenia4550.197 (0.105)0.1786 %+0.056 mm (p = 0.002)
    bipolar disorder4810.176 (0.111)0.1475 %+0.035 mm (p = 0.052)
    ADHD3910.134 (0.081)0.0982 %-0.007 mm (p = 0.66)
    In these data a person's mean head motion is linked (correlation, r = +0.48; 0 means no link and 1 means a perfect link) with their average hubness (motion inflates how much regions seem to rise and fall together). A group that fidgets more looks "different" almost everywhere. "Take head motion out first" regresses each person's mean FD out of their hubness before comparing.

    So why is everyone bad at this?

    The scores. Each diagnosis was told from the controls with the person held out. Schizophrenia reaches AUC 0.71 (shuffle p = 0.02 and head motion alone gives 0.67). Bipolar disorder reaches AUC 0.73 (shuffle p = 0.01 and head motion alone gives 0.59). ADHD reaches AUC 0.56 (shuffle p = 0.17 and head motion alone gives 0.46). An AUC of 0.50 is a coin flip and 1.00 is a crystal ball. The four-way computer you play against is right 50 % of the time. Dr. Nothing-Wrong is right 47 % of the time. A computer trained on shuffled labels gets 46 % by luck (95th percentile 47.2 %). Balanced over the four groups the computer scores 32 % where guessing gives 25 %. The four-way call is not much better than always saying "control volunteer". The one-vs-control scores for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (AUC 0.71 to 0.73) are a bit better than a coin flip, but not good enough to diagnose anyone.

    Why. A diagnosis is a name for a bundle of symptoms and not a thing you can point at in a brain. Two people with the same diagnosis can have wildly different brains. Medication, sleep, cigarettes and the sheer stress of being in a study all leave marks on a resting scan. The groups are small. There are 118 control volunteers, 45 with schizophrenia, 48 with bipolar disorder and 39 with ADHD. With 432 regions and groups that size a real but modest effect (d = 0.3) is invisible. The strictest correction for looking at 432 regions (Bonferroni) leaves one region standing, for schizophrenia, and none for the other two groups. That one region disappears once head motion is taken out first. One region is nowhere near enough to diagnose anyone. The smallest false-discovery q values are 0.03, 0.15 and 1.00. Head motion alone already scores an AUC of 0.67 (schizophrenia), 0.59 (bipolar disorder) and 0.46 (ADHD). And this is one five-minute scan averaged over a standard atlas with no symptoms, no history and no conversation.

    What scans do. MRI rules out the things that imitate psychiatric illness such as tumors, strokes and inflammation. It helps plan surgery. It does not diagnose schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or ADHD. A conversation with a person over time does that. Research scans like these are for understanding groups and not for judging a person. Anyone selling you a brain-scan diagnosis is selling you this page's coin flip. The people here volunteered so this question could be asked out loud. Nothing on this page says anything about any one of them.

    Toy warning: every number here is a whole-region average. The lab's real analyses use a stricter method called an fROI read. The model is one plain penalized logistic regression on 93,096 connections. There were 100 label shuffles so the smallest p we can report is 0.010. Every number was computed on the brain volume. The pictures are only pictures.

    How this was made (lab skills used)

    This panel is for the lab. It names the tools and steps we used, in the lab's own words.

    Data. The data are the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics LA5c study on OpenNeuro as ds000030. The raw release is Poldrack et al. 2016 (Sci Data) and the preprocessed release is Gorgolewski et al. 2017 (F1000Research). We used the fMRIPrep 1.0 resting-state BOLD in MNI152NLin2009cAsym plus the confounds and participants.tsv (diagnosis, age and gender). The voxels are 3 x 3 x 4 mm at TR 2 s for 152 volumes. That is about 5 min with eyes open. 261 people have a rest scan. 11 were left out for head motion above a mean FD of 0.5 mm (4 control volunteers, 5 with schizophrenia, 1 with bipolar disorder and 1 with ADHD). That leaves n = 250 (118 control volunteers, 45 with schizophrenia, 48 with bipolar disorder and 39 with ADHD).

    Pipeline. The scripts are in pipelines/doctor/. 01_parcel_timeseries.py takes region means over Schaefer-400 + SUIT cerebellum. That is 432 regions on this grid because the two fastigial nuclei vanish at 3 x 3 x 4 mm. The series are detrended and band-passed 0.01-0.1 Hz with 24 motion parameters (built from the 6 fMRIPrep wrote) + 5 aCompCor regressors in nilearn. 02_group_maps.py computes the Pearson correlation between every pair of regions and converts it to Fisher z. "Hubness" is a region's mean z to all others. The 8 x 8 grid is the mean z between networks. Each patient group is compared with the controls by Cohen's d and a Welch-t raw p per region. This is done with and without regressing mean FD out of hubness. It also counts Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg survivors and writes the motion table. 03_classify.py fits an L2 logistic regression on the 93,096 connections with 10-fold nested cross-validation. An inner 5-fold picks the penalty. It gives out-of-fold probabilities for every person. It fits one-vs-control models for each diagnosis (AUC) and one four-way model (the game's opponent). 100 label shuffles through the same folds give the permutation p. The same cross-validation on mean FD alone gives the motion-only AUC. 04_build_html.py builds this page.

    Lab skills used. The outlier skill supplied its framewise-displacement rule (FD > 0.5 mm marks a volume). It is computed per person in step 01 and reported as the "volumes > 0.5 mm" column. The exclusion itself follows the brief (mean FD > 0.5 mm). The sandbox skill supplied the per-unit resumable worker pattern from its template. Step 01 writes each subject with an atomic tmp-then-replace and leaves finished subjects alone. The lab's reporting convention is followed in the "Do the groups differ at all?" panel. That means raw p and the chance count beside any thresholded map and a stated correction. It comes from the project rules and not from a skill. The shared viewer (common/) draws the fsaverage5 brain pictures and the SUIT flatmap. Nothing is measured on them. The firstlevel and secondlevel skills were not used because there is no task. The froi-extract skill was not used because these are atlas region means and not fROIs. The surface-map and cerebellar-flatmap skills were not used because the shared viewer draws the pictures.

    Caveats. The Schaefer atlas is defined in MNI152NLin6Asym and applied to NLin2009cAsym data by header. That is about 1-2 mm off. It is fine for region means and not for anything finer. Region averages are whole-atlas-region means and not subject-specific functional ROIs. So this is a sketch of the connectome and not a lab-grade read. The groups differ in head motion, age and medication. None of these was matched or modeled in the classifier. The motion-only AUC is shown so the reader can see how much of the "signal" motion alone explains. 100 shuffles put the smallest reportable p at 0.010. Diagnoses are the study's clinical labels from SCID interviews. They are used here only as group labels and never to say anything about a person.

    These are real brains from OpenNeuro. The numbers come from the 3-D scans and the pretty pictures are only pictures. Hover or tap a region for its name.
